new_statements.quote: [Taine-Cheikh 2007 §2.1.6] Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb ‘desk’, on the second in mäktūb ‘written’. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics. || [Taine-Cheikh 2013 p. 22, identity] Actuellement les Imraguen parlent le ḥassāniyya, comme tous les Maures, mais certaines emplois lexicaux leur sont spécifiques.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages verified verbatim at the stated locators. (1), pdf p.5 = HAL preprint p.4, section '2.1.6 Stress', extracted text output reads exactly: 'Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb ‘desk’, on the second in mäktūb ‘written’. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics.' The surrounding section (2.1.2) also has the supporting line 'Long vowels have variable length: long under the accent, average apart from the accent, and short in final position.' new_statements.rule_in_words: In Hassaniyya Arabic (the actual speech of the Imraguen), word stress falls on the syllable containing the third mora counted from the end of the word (long vowels count two moras, so a penultimate long vowel attracts stress: mäktū́b; otherwise stress retracts, mä́ktäb); stress is realised mainly as length and is clearly audible only on long vowels; many grammatical morphemes are unstressed clitics.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in the EALL sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: None in §2.1.6; clitics noted as not bearing their own stress. (Taine-Cheikh 1988 BSL, held under hass1238, gives the fuller treatment of accentual units and clitics.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('from the end of the word'), citation forms; the statement describes Hassaniyya of Mauritania generally, not an Imraguen-specific variety — Taine-Cheikh 2013 says no such variety exists beyond specialised lexicon.
new_statements.identity_note: imer1236 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry; ISO 639-3 [ime] was retired 2015-01-12 (CR 2014-027, reason 'non-existent'). Taine-Cheikh 2013 (fieldworker on both Hassaniyya and Zenaga) states that the Imraguen fishermen of the Banc d'Arguin speak Hassaniyya Arabic like all Moors, with only some specialised (largely Zenaga-derived) fishing vocabulary and no trace of Azer; there is no separate Imraguen language and no separate phonology. The applicable word-stress description is therefore that of Hassaniyya Arabic, glottocode hass1238 (Taine-Cheikh 2007 EALL §2.1.6, already. A catalog entry under imer1236 would duplicate hass1238 (a retired code does not make a separate language).

sources.note: §2.1.6 Stress (preprint p. 4): 'Stress is on the third mora from the end of the word, e.g., on the first syllable in mäktäb, on the second in mäktūb. It is strongly marked only on long vowels (accent of length rather than intensity). A lot of grammatical morphemes are clitics.' Also §2.1.2: long vowels 'long under the accent, average apart from the accent, and short in final position'. This is the language the Imraguen speak.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. §4.2 (preprint p. 22): 'Actuellement les Imraguen parlent le ḥassāniyya, comme tous les Maures, mais certaines emplois lexicaux leur sont spécifiques.' Conclusion (p. 26): hunters and fishers 'ne présentent pas de spécificités linguistiques telles qu'elles puissent servir de base à une revendication ethnique propre'; Gerteiny's 'Hassaniyya on an Azer base' is rejected, Imraguen special lexicon is Hassaniyya + Zenaga, no attested Azer.
